title: Touring life: rooming, flying, and George Lewis's American popularity
summary: Who roomed together, Jim Robinson's fear of flying, crowds at the Paramount, Louis Armstrong and George, and the college dates.

story.theme_name: Life on the road: touring bands, buses and one-nighters
story.community_name: Life on the road: buses, trains and one-nighters

blocks.x: Oh, no. I mean, how, uh, who shared rooms together? Oh, I, I don't know. I always tried to see to it that George had a room to himself.

Because he was not in good health. He was in very frail health. And he had to sleep in the daytime and, uh, uh, get all the sleep. And I always tried to see if we couldn't work it that way. Drag and, uh, well, Drag and Joe Watkins always shared the room. Mm-hm. And let me see, uh, Elton Bernal. Well, then it just, but it was pretty standard, the Drag and, that Drag and Joe. Mm-hm. And George, whenever we possibly could, I'm trying to get him a room to himself. And then, I guess, the others, as I recall, it was... Jim Robinson or Kit Howard. Oh, yes. Jim Robinson and Kit Howard. That's true. Mm-hm. And then, I think, Elton and Lawrence quite often. Oh. Quite often. Did they have any special things that they would do on tour? I mean, did any, like, you know, particular job or something that had to be done would be done particularly by one person? No. Did they have anything like that? Well, no. They all, they had enough to do taking care of their instruments. Mm-hm. You know, Joe keeping track of his drums. Because I, I would keep track of them insofar as, uh, checking them, you know, and transportation and all that. But they, they, there was, there was plenty to do with, just as I say, keeping track of their instruments. And, no, no, nobody had any particular, uh, job. Did they, did they travel mainly by train or, or how would they live? Well, in those days, well, train or plane. Train or plane. They were, they were, I wouldn't have thought maybe at that time they would have been flying so much more. Oh yes, we, we flew a good deal. Yes, we, uh. Did they, did any of them have any particular aversion to that? Yes. Yes, Jim Robinson was terrified. Was one? It was, I think I have one here. It was his, his first plane trip and I don't remember what two cities, I don't remember what flight it was, but I do remember for some reason that it was on TWA. And, uh, he really was. He was, he was terribly apprehensive. And I had with me some very mild sedative pills. I don't know, I don't think they would really have affected a kitten. And, uh, but I gave it to him. And apparently it was the psychological effect. Because the pill itself could have had no effect. Mm-hm. And, uh, Jim kind of let out a sigh of relief, put his head back and fell asleep. And I'm sure it wasn't the, uh, pill I gave him. Um, what, uh, what do you, what is your impression on, or general feeling about the extent of George's popularity in America? Well, I think he has a hard core of fanatic fans. Uh, you only have to see them lined up outside those clubs in, in San Francisco and Chicago. In fact, anywhere. In fact, anywhere. You had only to see the crowds in New York. Pack them in. However. Where was this in New York? At the Paramount. Yes, that's the, uh, and that was, that's a huge place. Um, of course it's no longer there. Where was that? It was, uh, under the old Paramount Theater on Broadway. By Times Square, is that? Right by the Times building. The Times newspaper. And, uh, that place every weekend, not during the week, but weekends, that place was packed to the walls. How many people did it have? Six hundred and something. Good heavens. Yeah, it was a very large place. And, of course, at the Beverly Cavern in the Royal Room, they'd line up outside. Hmm. And, to get tables. And, uh, the same way, they got big crowds in Chicago. Everywhere he went. He drew them. But that does not necessarily mean that the younger people who don't know this music, uh, uh, I would say that George's popularity in this country is, is, uh, unequaled for, uh, or this rock bottom true jazz. That there isn't anybody who can, uh, better him. And I realize there's a man named Louis Armstrong. But, uh, uh, uh, he is no longer... No. ...represents that particular, what George represents. Right. Because George's music has never changed. And, um, uh, uh, oh, yes, I'd say he's popular among those who are New Orleans jazz, what they call buffs. Do you know if Louis Armstrong ever heard George Lewis play? Oh, mercy, yes. In this period? I mean, no. Of course, when he was back in the old days in New Orleans, he may have, well, even then he probably may have known. No, he didn't. You see, Louis left New Orleans when he was about 17 years old. Right. George never left until he was 45. Right. But, uh, uh, I'm sure Louis has heard him in, uh, well, in fact, I think Louis went to some of his concerts in London. Oh, is that right? Mm-hmm. Louis and he were in London at, uh, I think one engagement was, Louis was playing one concert, and I don't recall, but I'm, I'm, I'm very sure that he heard him in London. I know we heard Louis, and George always went backstage, and, uh, Louis is very fond of George. He sees things in the world. And, uh, Louis had a, I remember a young man, a fan of George's from Cincinnati, and, uh, he was, uh, at an Armstrong concert, and he wanted to, uh, he wanted to see Louis, he wanted to meet him. And, uh, uh, they wouldn't let him in backstage, you know, that Louis had, uh, the, the, you know, how the situation backstage can be. So, this chap had a, um, photograph of George Lewis with him. He took a scrap of paper and he wrote, friend of, on it, clipped it to the picture of George Lewis, and sent it in, and Louis didn't say bring him in. Louis came out to meet him, and brought him in himself. Um, and, um. I once heard a rumor, and I think this was just a rumor, that, that, that, that Louis had, at one point, considered, or even said something about having George Lewis playing his band. If he did, I never knew anything about it. No, I don't. No, I don't, I don't think that's true. Uh, unless Louis may have mentioned it to somebody, um, I know he never mentioned it to George. Uh, I would, I would say that was one of the multitudinous rumors that spring up in the jazz world. Yes. Because I knew nothing about it. Yes. Because I knew nothing about it. What do you think the, uh, impression that George Lewis band made on the kind of younger college audiences that he was playing for in that time? They loved it. Oh, they loved it. They loved it. Oh. Oh. Where were some of the college places you played? Okay. There, there was Ohio State, Purdue, Brown, that'd be in the East, um, college in Vermont. Oh dear.
